articles.title: A Texas homeowners association meeting ended in a physical fight between a resident recording the proceedings and the volunteer treasurer; an appeals court ruled the association was not responsible for the altercation
articles.summary: A homeowners association is not legally responsible for a physical fight between one of its residents and its volunteer treasurer, a Texas appeals court
articles.body: A homeowners association is not legally responsible for a physical fight between one of its residents and its volunteer treasurer, a Texas appeals court has ruled. The dispute began after a heated exchange at a Lake Bonanza Property Owners Association meeting, where a resident started recording the proceedings. The situation led to a physical fight between the resident and the association's elected treasurer, who was a volunteer rather than an employee. On November 12, 2026, the Thirteenth Court of Appeals of Texas upheld an earlier ruling in favour of the homeowners association. The appeals court found that the volunteer treasurer's physical actions were not part of his duties or authority as a board member.According to the court's written opinion, the people involved were resident Rodney Snell and the association's treasurer, identified as Courtney in court documents. The incident took place during or after a budget meeting of the Lake Bonanza Property Owners Association in Montgomery County. Snell had started recording the meeting, a common practice at community gatherings that can sometimes lead to disagreements. The physical fight that followed between Snell and Courtney led Snell to file a personal injury lawsuit against Lake Bonanza Property Owners Association, Inc.Snell wanted the association to be held legally responsible for the actions of its elected volunteer board member. This type of legal responsibility is known as vicarious liability, often called respondeat superior. It is a legal rule that can make an employer or organisation responsible for the actions of an employee or representative when those actions happen as part of their job or official duties.Examining the treasurer’s scope of volunteer dutiesThe main question before the Thirteenth Court of Appeals was whether Courtney's actions during the physical fight were part of the authority given to him by the association. The judges looked at whether his actions were "within the scope of the . . . general authority in furtherance of the [principal's] business and for the accomplishment of the object for which the [agent] was hired." The court also examined what it means to be "hired" when someone holds an elected volunteer position. Vicarious liability usually applies to relationships between employers and employees. However, the court noted that it can also apply when an organisation has the right to control someone acting on its behalf.The opinion explained that Snell argued vicarious liability could apply because an organisation has the right to control its representative, even when there is no formal employment relationship. He also appeared to argue that "there should be no dispute . . . Courtney was an agent" of Lake Bonanza simply because he was its elected treasurer. However, the court concluded that holding the elected position of treasurer was not enough by itself to establish the legal requirements for vicarious liability. To decide whether Lake Bonanza could be held responsible for Courtney's physical actions, the judges examined whether the fight was connected to his duties as treasurer. The opinion stated that "record evidence indicates this discussion did not occur during the board meeting or as part of Courtney's duties as treasurer."Differentiating volunteer status from an employee relationshipSnell also made several other arguments to show that the association was directly responsible through negligence. The court considered whether Courtney was under the association's control when the disagreement with Snell took place. The appeals court reviewed the case under a standard known as de novo. This means the judges examined the legal issues themselves without having to follow the lower court's reasoning. To grant summary judgment, a party must show that "no genuine issue of material fact exists and that it is entitled to judgment as a matter of law," the court explained.Snell argued that the association was directly negligent. According to the court's opinion, proving this required evidence "of a legal duty, breach of that duty, and damages proximately resulting from the breach." Snell also claimed that the association had failed in its duties when hiring and training Courtney. The court rejected these arguments. It found "no evidence Lake Bonanza either hired Courtney, trained him in any capacity or had any duty to train him, or had any duty to supervise him."The judges also pointed out that Snell had not provided any legal authority showing that elected board members have a relationship with their associations similar to the relationship between employees and employers. Such a relationship would be important to support his direct negligence claims. The court concluded that Snell had "failed to produce more than a scintilla of evidence to support his claim of negligent hiring and training." It therefore upheld the summary judgment on the claims of direct liability as well. The association successfully showed that it was not legally responsible for the physical fight. As a result, the Thirteenth Court of Appeals upheld the lower court's decision that Snell could recover nothing from Lake Bonanza Property Owners Association, Inc.You use AI every day. articles.title: Europe and Ukraine get a boost in peace talks, but Putin is playing for time
articles.summary: The Russians appear to have agreed to give Europe a seat at the negotiating table. Whether it spurs progress towards peace remains to be seen
articles.body: At the airport in a freezing Moscow, the billionaire property developer and one of President Donald Trump’s top envoys, Steve Witkoff, fielded a brief question from a CNN team that had been ushered onto the tarmac. Yes, there had been “progress” at the talks that day with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Witkoff answered. “This is what President Trump wants to see,” he added, hinting at how keen the US leader remains on scoring a diplomatic win in the brutal five-year conflict he once bragged he would end in a day. That progress is European involvement. For nearly two years, Europe has been effectively sidelined in talks with Russia to bring about peace in Ukraine. But now, after Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner met President Putin in Moscow on Thursday, the Russians appear to have agreed to give Europe a seat at the negotiating table, something previously resisted by Moscow. The move was welcomed by the Ukrainian President, Volodymyr Zelensky, who has become increasingly dependent on European military, diplomatic and financial support to keep his country afloat and Russian forces at bay. “It is important that Europeans, next time, next meeting, Europe will be on the negotiating team, not somewhere, not separately. They will have a voice,” Zelensky told reporters in Ireland, after being briefed by Kushner and Witkoff at a meeting of European leaders. “This is important to us because the war is in Europe. We will be a member of the EU in the future and that is why it is very important. For prosperity and for security guarantees, it is very important to have Europe,” Zelensky added. The Europeans, while deeply skeptical about Russia’s commitment to finding a diplomatic solution to end the Ukraine war, see the inclusion of a European element in future peace talks as a positive step, as well as a long-overdue acknowledgement that Washington can’t do it alone. “I think that after almost two years of talks between the US and Russia, they have now realized that Europe is a big player here,” Kaja Kallas, the EU’s top diplomat, commented in Dublin. “We are the ones who have been supporting Ukraine, and we are the ones who have put sanctions in place, and we have the frozen (Russian) assets. So, clearly, without us, any agreement that is there cannot be implemented,” she added. The makeup of Europe’s delegation has been the subject of fierce internal debate. On Friday, the President of the European Council António Costa said the European team would be represented by the EU institutions and the E5 nations of France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the UK. Earlier, Kushner highlighted potential difficulties with Europe being able to “identify one person to speak on their behalf,” saying that to do so “would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiation.” The formal involvement of European negotiators may be lauded in Kyiv and Brussels, but it won’t necessarily hasten the end of a conflict that is estimated to have killed hundreds of thousands of people on both sides so far. In later remarks, Russia steered clear of admitting they had fully agreed to a European presence at the table. In his regular briefing on Friday, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Europe must show its “willingness to contribute to the peace process” before a decision could be made on letting them join future negotiations. European leaders routinely take a hard and moral line against Moscow, often calling for Russia to be defeated and punished for launching its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and for the Kremlin to withdraw its troops from all Ukrainian territory. If those mantras are merely repeated at the negotiating table and more practical compromise suggestions from Europe are not forthcoming, a breakthrough with the Kremlin will become even less likely, as Moscow has indicated. “They (the Europeans) must decide whether they want peace or the continuation of the war. So far, all their practical actions point precisely to the latter,” said Yuri Ushakov in a briefing to reporters after the meetings in Moscow. And there are early signs that Moscow, having agreed to admit European negotiators, is already doubling down on its maximalist demands to end the war, reviving its call for NATO to withdraw from eastern Europe, and digging in its heels on the issue of the potential deployment of peacekeepers to police any ceasefire along the frontlines. “The way out that the American administration and President Trump have to offer is about coming to terms on prospective arrangements for pan-European security. And what do we hear from the Europeans? They’ve been saying no. Only after the peace deal in Ukraine is done,” President Putin told Witkoff and Kushner in a televised snapshot of the talks. “But after that peace deal is done in Ukraine, they… they’re going to deploy their troops, which would mean a continuation of the war. So this is a vicious circle,” Putin continued. It’s a sign the Kremlin, even if it does not welcome European involvement in negotiations, will find a way of using that new reality to try and reach its objectives in Ukraine, not least by stretching out further talks while pounding Ukrainian cities. Another winter of bitter conflict, one last push, is probably what the Kremlin really wants.

articles.title: School investigating after viral video shows 10th-grade girl punched, put in chokehold on Ohio school bus
articles.summary: Viral video shows a male student repeatedly punching, kicking and choking a 10th-grade girl on an Ohio school bus as other students laughed.
articles.body: An Ohio school board is investigating an attack on a 10th-grade girl by a male student on a school bus after video of the assault went viral on social media. The incident occurred Friday, Nov. 6, on a school bus taking students to the Mahoning Valley Community School, a public high school in Youngstown that serves students from grades 7 to 12. The video, apparently filmed by another student on the bus, showed a boy repeatedly punching and kicking the girl. Other students could be heard laughing until the boy put her in a chokehold, prompting someone to say, "Chill." The girl's stepfather told WKBN-TV that he found out how everything happened on Wednesday, five days after the brutal beating she suffered. He said she was taken to the hospital to check the severity of her injuries. Under that arrangement, the district provides bus transportation for MVCS students. The district released a statement to FOX 8, a Cleveland TV affiliate, apologizing for "the delay in promptly notifying parents of the incident." "While bus staff notified Community School administrators, the severity of the incident was not adequately communicated," the district added. "We can share that no student injuries were reported following the incident. We are reviewing both notification and transportation procedures to determine what happened and whether improvements are needed." "This is a complete failure to communicate, protect. I don’t even have the words — there are so many to use," he added. articles.title: At least 10 killed in Guinea clashes over gold mining ban
articles.summary: Guinea banned artisanal gold mining in Siguiri on November 2 due to environmental degradation, causing mass exodus.
articles.body:
At least 10 people have been killed and 13 others injured in clashes in northeastern Guinea between protesters and security forces enforcing restrictions on gold mining, the government said.

The country’s Ministry of Territorial ‌Administration said late on Thursday that clashes occurred on Wednesday, when defence and security forces were verifying the implementation of a ban on artisanal gold mining.

The violence erupted in Balato, in the Siguiri region, during a patrol against illegal and unregulated gold mining. Protesters erected barricades blocking the patrol, as the situation escalated into clashes and exchanges of gunfire, the statement said. It did not specify who opened fire.

Ten people, including five foreign nationals whose identities have yet to be established, were among those killed. The injured included civilians and members of the security forces.

Two pick-up trucks and a security forces truck were burned, while a firearm and a motorcycle were taken by protesters, the ministry said.

Judicial authorities have been tasked with establishing what triggered the violence and determining responsibility.

Guinea banned artisanal gold mining in Siguiri on November 2. Authorities said artisanal miners’ failure to comply with regulations had led to environmental degradation, including pollution of agricultural land, rivers and vegetation ⁠cover.

Neighbouring Mali said last week that around 100,000 people had arrived in the capital Bamako and nearly 60,000 more in the border town of Kouremale after they ⁠were forced to leave Guinea when the ban on artisanal mining was announced.

Burkina Faso said on Friday it had repatriated 45,406 of ⁠its citizens, who were forced to leave Guinea as a result of the ban.

Artisanal mining, driven by growing demand ⁠for metals and rising prices, is a common activity across much of West Africa.

Artisanal and small-scale gold mining supports the livelihoods of more than 300,000 people in Guinea, according to the UN Environment Programme.

But the Guinean government said the restrictions aim to curb environmental damage from mining, including the destruction of farmland by heavy machinery and the pollution of rivers by chemicals.

Authorities arrested more than 1,200 people suspected of illegal gold mining in the Siguiri region earlier this month, according to authorities, with the first mass trials opened this week.

articles.title: Eurovision Song Contest is finally coming to Asia - meet the stars gearing up in Thailand
articles.summary: On Saturday, the biggest and longest-running international song contest will make a leap into unknown territory.
articles.body:
On Saturday, the biggest and longest-running international song contest will make a leap into unknown territory.

Eurovision, the pan-European competition famed for zany gimmicks, slick, sometimes over-the-top staging, the drama of its complex voting system and, occasionally, for outstanding music, celebrates its 70th birthday this year.

And to mark it, the European Broadcasting Union is trying out audiences in Asia.

It's an idea that's been talked about for two decades but never materialised, despite many false starts.

Until now - Eurovision Asia will hold its first grand final in Bangkok, starting at 20:30 ICT (13:30 GMT).

Transferring one of the most successful television formulas that has worked in Europe for 70 years to Asia has not been straightforward, says Sarun 'Note' Kungbunpot, a Eurovision enthusiast and Thai singer who has won several competitions in this region.

"It's still very new in Asia. I'm not sure many people have heard about it yet," he says, adding that he thinks it will take a bit of time for audiences to adjust.

"When we look at contests in Thailand, the Philippines and Korea, we actually compete based on the singer.

"It's all about popularity – fans are looking for their idols. But Eurovision is all about the song, not the singer. I think this needs to be communicated clearly."

Then there is the long history of Eurovision in Europe. It began in 1956 as a project to encourage greater cultural exchanges in a Europe which was trying to forge a common future after two world wars.

This was the very start of the age of mass television ownership, and Eurovision became such a fixture it is now an indelible piece of Europe's shared cultural heritage. It has no such resonance in Asia, and arrives in this region in the digital age, when traditional TV formats are struggling to cut through.

Only 11 countries are taking part in this first Eurovision Asia contest – host Thailand, along with Malaysia, the Philippines, Vietnam, Cambodia, Laos, South Korea, Mongolia, Bangladesh, Nepal and Bhutan.

Asian giants India, China, Japan and Indonesia are noticeably absent, although there are negotiations ongoing to try to get them into next year's contest, assuming there is one.

There have also been problems with the organisation of this event.

A sudden million-dollar (£760,000) budget cut just three weeks before the final meant many of the technicians familiar with staging Eurovision were not brought to Thailand, and there have been a number of staff resignations too.

Eurovision fans - and there are many passionate followers around the world - have noticed, criticising audio and lighting in rehearsal videos.

The contest's unusual voting system will be unfamiliar to Asian audiences. Like in Europe, Eurovision Asia will determine the winner through a 50/50 mix of public voting and national juries from each of the 11 contesting countries, as well as a 12th "rest of the world" category.

Anyone can vote - you get eight votes once you register - but you cannot vote for your own country's contestant and you must give your votes to at least three others.

The public and jury votes are then converted into points. The most popular song among the Bhutanese or Mongolians, for example, will get 12 points from those countries, while the song ranked last will get zero - the famous "nul points".

In Europe, there have long been reports of co-ordinated voting to back neighbours, for example the four Nordic countries voting for each other. This seems less likely in Eurovision Asia, but political differences, for example between Thailand and Cambodia after their border war last year, could influence how their audiences vote.

Filipinos, with their passion for singing, are expected to be enthusiastic participants and the 11 million who live overseas might make a difference. But as most live and work in countries which are not participating, their votes will only go into the "rest of the world" pool.

For Bhutan, with a population of less than a million, this is a rare chance to shine on a global stage, which puts some pressure on 24-year-old Thukten Nyendra, the singer representing the Himalayan kingdom in Bangkok with his song Lhayi Semo (The Angel). Before coming here he had never left his country or been on a plane before.

"I'm not a star. I'm just Nyendra over there," he told the BBC. "Nobody knows me. But Eurovision has given me a huge platform. Actually winning would mean the world to us... If I really make it through all of this, it would mean the entire freaking world to us."

The other characteristic of Eurovision is the song format – no more than three minutes, no more than six people on stage, and no backing band, only taped music.

This encourages performers to prepare elaborate, sometimes outrageous choreography and stunts to impress the audience – think Poland's My Słowianie in 2014 with models in traditional costume churning butter on stage, or the Finnish heavy metal band Lordi donning flamboyant monster outfits in its 2006 entry.

There has also been a long association of Eurovision with LGBTQ+ artists. Eurovision Asia includes Malaysia and Bangladesh – where same-sex activity is illegal – and there are no visible LGBTQ+ elements this year.

Performers have been using the last days of rehearsals before the final to try to make their stage acts as striking as possible. Thinla from Laos has abandoned the short, sequinned dress she wore in the first video of her infectious reggaeton song Bae and is adopting Lao hill-tribe costume for her and her backing dancers.

Perhaps the most ambitious choreography is in Vietnamese singer Tóc Tiên's song Em Tiên ("Fairy Maiden").

It has been exhausting just watching her rehearse the elaborate moves and costume changes for more than an hour at a time.

The entry from Bangladesh's Beatmosphere, Tumi Ele ("You Came"), is unusual as an a cappella and beatboxing performance by six men with little backing music.

The youngest contestant is 19 year-old Carmelle Collado from the Philippines, whose bubbling confidence and strong stage presence in her song Sobra-Sobra ("Too Much") belie her youth.

"I'm actually quite scared because I'm the youngest, but also really happy," she told us.

"The song is about feminine energy. It's about being brave, strong, fierce, and it's about how strong Filipino women are."

Eurovision is famous for putting unknown acts onto a global stage, and introducing musicians who went on to become megastars – think Abba, little known when they won in 1974 with Waterloo, and Celine Dion winning in Ireland in 1988.

Because of the lack of public awareness of Eurovision Asia many of the finalists chosen for this first contest are already well known in their home markets.

Aina Abdul is perhaps the most famous singer in Malaysia, known as much for dramatic costumes as her impressive vocal range. Her song Bluest Sky – which she told us was inspired by her late cat Hiro – is a strong contender to win the contest.

Abdul's spectacular dress, by Malaysian designer Melinda Looi, who has travelled to Bangkok with her, had taken 600 hours to make, she told me. She said its glistening texture, made from materials brought from Italy and China, is meant to represent moving water.

If all goes well on the night, the organisers are hoping this could be the start of an expansion of the hugely successful Eurovision brand into a region which, after all, has half the world's population.

articles.title: Alex Murdaugh wants murder indictments tossed, saying agent lied
articles.summary: Alex Murdaugh is facing a retrial on murder charges after the South Carolina Supreme Court threw out his convictions and life sentence.
articles.body:
Attorneys for Alex Murdaugh asked a judge Friday to throw out the original murder indictments for killing his wife and son, saying the chief investigator in the case lied to the grand jury.

Murdaugh is facing a retrial on the murder charges after the South Carolina Supreme Court threw out his convictions and life sentence, ruling that a court clerk improperly influenced jurors against him during his 2023 trial .

Even if the request to dismiss the indictments is granted, it may not stop or even postpone an April retrial for the disgraced lawyer. Prosecutors can seek another set of grand jury indictments, and defense attorneys said they won't stop them.

Judge ends hearing with interesting question

Judge Debra McCaslin did not immediately decide on the defense request, promising a written ruling next week. But one of her last comments at the hearing may have indicated where she is going.

"If you had to go back to the grand jury, could you have it all done and ready to go by April 5th?" she asked prosecutor Creighton Waters.

"Your honor, I'm always working ahead," Waters responded.

Throwing out indictments could be another rebuke of agent on case

A ruling throwing out the indictments would be another rebuke of the chief investigator in Murdaugh's case, State Law Enforcement Division agent David Owen.

A judge last year threw out a different murder case Owen was involved in because the dead woman's mother told the agent about a suicide threat her daughter made days before she died that Owen never relayed to prosecutors or defense attorneys. She was found dead by the same method she told her mother she was going to use to kill herself.

Owen abruptly retired in 2024, not long after he was honored as State Law Enforcement Officer of the Year.

Prosecutors pointed out while Owen is accused of hiding or not revealing evidence in that case, all the issues in the Murdaugh case involved evidence and reports the defense had at the original trial.

The grand jury heard several questionable assertions

Prosecutors said Murdaugh, 58, killed his wife, Maggie, and younger son, Paul, on their sprawling property in the South Carolina Lowcountry in 2021. Murdaugh is spending decades in prison for stealing millions of dollars from clients, and has admitted in court that he is a thief, insurance cheat, bad lawyer and longtime opioid addict. But he denies being a killer.

Defense lawyers said that as prosecutors sought the indictments, Owen told the Colleton County grand jury that blood spatter was found on a T-shirt Murdaugh was wearing the night of the killings. An earlier report from state agents said there were no blood stains, and no such evidence was introduced at trial.

Owen also told grand jurors that the same ammunition load of buckshot in one chamber and large birdshot in the other used to kill Paul Murdaugh was found loaded in weapons all over the Murdaugh property, which wasn't the case.

The grand jury may have heard about plenty of evidence, including the video Paul Murdaugh recorded in which Alex Murdaugh's voice could be heard at the scene, contradicting his claims that he wasn't at the kennels near where his wife and son were killed any time close to their deaths.

But defense attorney Jim Griffin said the false evidence of the blood of Murdaugh's son was the only thing anyone heard that could link him to the place and time of the killings.

"A phone call doesn't put him there. The video doesn't put him there," Griffin said. "The blood from his murdered son sprang through the air — it's raining back on him — puts him there."

Prosecutors call it a mistake, cite other evidence against Murdaugh

Prosecutors said they had plenty of other evidence supporting the murder charges, and wrote in court papers that "a single mistake is not bad faith."

Along with the kennel video, Owen told the grand jury about the family's mounting debts, guns missing from the house that matched what could have been used in the killings and how Murdaugh's schemes to steal from clients and his law firm were close to being discovered.

"This is what the agent understood at the time. And it's ultimately not something that would cause a substantial effect on the grand jury or cast grave doubt when we look at all the other evidence that was presented," Waters said.

Prosecutors said Murdaugh killed his wife and son because he thought the sympathy generated by the killings would buy him time to cover up his thefts.

Murdaugh's lawyers have repeatedly pointed out how little evidence prosecutors have. No DNA or blood was found splattered on Murdaugh or any of his clothes, even though the killings were at close range with powerful weapons that were never found.

"What we're asking, your honor, is to reboot — go back to square one," Griffin said.

Even with the original convictions overturned, Murdaugh remains in prison on separate financial crime sentences . The outcome of the murder case will not determine when he could be released.

articles.title: A Missouri hotel guest's truck slid into a van on an icy parking lot, then he fell while photographing the damage; after his injury lawsuit was dismissed, a November 10 appeals court revived his claim against Motel 6
articles.summary: An icy parking lot turned an early-morning vehicle accident into a personal injury dispute after a hotel guest slipped and injured his shoulder while
articles.body: An icy parking lot turned an early-morning vehicle accident into a personal injury dispute after a hotel guest slipped and injured his shoulder while photographing damage to another vehicle. Although the entire parking area had experienced freezing conditions, the guest argued that the spot where he fell was particularly dangerous because of uncleared snow, accumulated ice and deep tyre tracks. A lower court dismissed his lawsuit, but a Missouri appeals court has now found that the circumstances required further examination.In an opinion issued on November 10, 2026, the Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District, reversed the summary judgment granted to Super 6 Inn, LLC, which operates the Motel 6 property in Kingdom City. In Jeff Woosley v. Super 6 Inn, LLC., d/b/a Motel 6, the court ruled that factual disputes remained over whether the hotel had allowed an artificially dangerous condition to develop in part of its parking lot. The decision, available on Justia, sends the case back to the lower court for further proceedings.Truck slid into a parked van on icy morningAccording to the court's opinion, Jeff Woosley was staying at the Motel 6 on Jade Road in Kingdom City on the night of January 21-22, 2024. He was working as a maintenance training instructor at a nearby nuclear power plant. The hotel's parking lot had two sections: a concrete area with designated spaces for passenger vehicles and an adjoining gravel area used by larger trucks and cargo vehicles.The concrete section had been cleared following an earlier winter storm, but the gravel section had not received similar treatment. Snow removed from the concrete area had also been pushed towards the boundary between the two sections. Vehicles using the gravel area had created deep ruts in the accumulated snow and ice.On the morning of January 22, freezing rain and sleet began falling shortly after midnight. At around 6am, Woosley went outside to start his truck before returning to his room to let it warm up. When he came back approximately 20 minutes later and attempted to leave, his truck began sliding on the inclined, icy concrete surface. It struck a white work van parked partly on the concrete and partly on the gravel.Woosley initially inspected the damage and returned inside to contact the Highway Patrol. After learning that an officer would take some time to arrive, he asked the hotel attendant for information about the van's owner.Guest fell while photographing the damageBetween 6.30am and 7am, Woosley returned outside to photograph the damage and obtain the van's registration number. It was still dark. While recording the accident scene with his phone, he walked from the concrete parking area onto the adjoining gravel section. His foot slipped on the uneven, icy surface, and he fell, striking his left shoulder against the ground.He later drove approximately three hours to an emergency room in St. Joseph for medical treatment. Woosley subsequently filed a negligence and premises liability lawsuit against the hotel. He alleged that it had failed to properly remove snow and ice or apply ice-melting treatment, leaving the parking area unsafe for guests.Why the lower court dismissed the lawsuitSuper 6 Inn argued that it had no legal duty to remove naturally accumulating snow and ice during an ongoing winter storm. It relied on the Massachusetts Rule, a legal principle recognised in Missouri that generally protects property owners from liability for injuries caused by natural accumulations of snow and ice resulting from weather conditions affecting the wider community.The hotel also argued that the icy conditions were open and obvious because Woosley had already encountered the slippery parking lot several times before falling. The Callaway County Circuit Court accepted these arguments and granted summary judgment to the hotel in August 2025, dismissing the lawsuit. Woosley appealed, arguing that the court had overlooked the different conditions in the concrete and gravel sections.Appeals court found a factual disputeThe appeals court agreed that the lower court had not properly considered the specific location where Woosley fell. The judges noted that his earlier trips had been across the concrete section, whereas his fall occurred on the separate gravel surface. His awareness of general icy conditions did not automatically establish that he knew about the particular danger created by packed snow and uneven tyre tracks.The court also found that the Massachusetts Rule did not necessarily protect the hotel. Evidence suggested that its failure to clear the earlier snowfall, the movement of snow from the concrete area and vehicle traffic over the untreated gravel could have created a localised, artificially dangerous condition. These circumstances raised genuine factual questions that could not be resolved through summary judgment.What happens nextThe Missouri Court of Appeals reversed the lower court's judgment and remanded the case for further proceedings. All three judges agreed with the decision. The ruling does not establish that Motel 6 was negligent or that Woosley is entitled to compensation. It means only that his claims should not have been dismissed at this stage because the evidence raised questions requiring further examination.The case highlights the distinction between naturally occurring winter weather conditions and additional hazards that may develop when property owners fail to maintain particular areas of their premises.You use AI every day. articles.title: Europe to send a diplomat team to Ukraine talks as leaders push for a voice
articles.summary: Europe will send a team of diplomats from the European Union and five individual countries to the next round of Ukraine talks, a top E.U. official said Friday.
articles.body: DUBLIN — Europe will send a team of diplomats from the European Union and five individual countries to the next round of Ukraine talks, a top E.U. official said Friday after a summit focused on how to avoid being shut out of U.S.-led negotiations on ending the nearly five-year war. European Council President Antonio Costa said the continent will be represented by officials from the 27-nation E.U. bloc and five members of the “Coalition of the Willing” that backs Ukraine: the U.K., France, Germany, Italy and Poland. “We need to integrate all of us. And for this it’s essential to have a team and to speak with only one voice,” Costa said. European leaders have been concerned that a U.S.-backed process will leave them sidelined and Kyiv vulnerable as Moscow and Washington decide the fate of a conflict that has roiled the continent. Ukraine is eager for support from its European allies. It’s reluctant to leave the talks solely in the hands of a U.S. administration that has often seemed to lean toward Moscow’s views. Russia does not want European countries involved in direct negotiations, complaining they are financing and supplying Ukraine’s military effort. European leaders also distrust U.S. President Donald Trump to negotiate on their behalf after a series of tense standoffs over trade, Greenland and conflicts in Iran and Ukraine. “Without Europeans, there is no support for Ukraine,” French President Emmanuel Macron said Thursday at a meeting of the European Political Community in Dublin. “There is no more U.S. support.” “At the end of the day, we will be the ones to define and decide for our future security as Europeans,” he said. Europe is broadly aligned but not unified European leaders fear Russian President Vladimir Putin will press Trump to back a peace settlement that weakens not just Ukraine but broader European security. Putin has demanded NATO troops be pulled back from Russia’s borders and that no European forces be deployed in Ukraine. As envoys from Washington, Moscow and Kyiv met this week in Abu Dhabi, several European countries, including the U.K., France and Germany, attended discussions nearby, but not the main talks. U.S. envoy Jared Kushner and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said after they met in Dublin late Thursday that Europe would be part of the next round of talks. Zelenskyy said Europe would send a negotiating team, adding, “They will have a voice.” “We cannot conclude this deal without the Europeans being at the table,” Kushner said. He said Putin “is willing to give it a try.” An old question with no simple answer European leaders are united in wanting a place at the table. But they have tussled over whether Europe should be represented by one person — as Russia has demanded and the U.S. suggested it would prefer — or a team. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Thursday that “the Europeans squabble like spiders in a jar” and they should name a representative. Supporters of a single envoy, such as Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, argued that the absence of a united European voice has allowed individual countries or small groups to engage in freelance diplomacy. “There are too many different groupings discussing the issue,” she said. The question of who represents Europe is an old one. Europe itself is loosely defined. Is it the 27-nation EU, the 32-nation NATO military alliance made up mostly of European countries, the 29-nation Schengen zone, or the 47-nation European Political Community? That has long frustrated Washington. After this week’s U.S.-brokered talks between Ukraine and Russia in the United Arab Emirates, Kushner said that “if Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiation.” That echoes the famous question often misattributed to former U.S. Secretary of State Henry Kissinger: “Who do I call if I want to call Europe?” A team of envoys from the E.U. and beyond The decision to send a team, rather than an individual, allows for participation by members of the “coalition of the willing,” a group of nations that have pledged to underpin a future ceasefire with military support. That includes the U.K., which left the EU in 2020. Poland is a voice for nations on the E.U.’s eastern flank that face constant hybrid threats from Russia, including influence campaigns and disruptive drones. It was not immediately clear who would represent the E.U.’s institutions. Speculation had centered on Costa and the E.U.’s top diplomat, Kaja Kallas. Earlier this year, Costa faced criticism within the E.U. after his office set up a hush-hush back-channel with Moscow. Kallas, a former prime minister of Estonia, laid claim to the envoy role Friday, saying, “I’m the one who is representing Europe in the foreign and security policy.” “I know that the Russians don’t want me, but, you know, do we have a say, who is representing Russia?” she said. “We can’t send any person that has no institutional role like the Americans are sending.” Some leaders deeply distrust the U.S.-brokered talks. “In my opinion, calling them negotiations is an exaggeration,” Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Thursday. “We will not build a new security architecture simply because the Russian president, or someone in the United States, wishes it.” With Trump due to head to Beijing next week to meet Putin, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said European leaders feared another “Anchorage moment,” a reference to the Alaska summit where they were stunned by Trump’s overtures to the Russian leader in the absence of Ukrainian or European envoys. “Please, no surprises,” Merz said. “Continue to play in team Europe and in the team with Ukraine.” Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs noted that Europe is larger than Russia in population, economy and military might. “We as Europe have to grow some bigger balls,” he said.

articles.title: Indian PhD student Bilal Kazi jailed in UK for 30 years for preying on young girls on Snapchat. He was overstaying his student visa
articles.summary: 27-year-old Bilal Kazi, an Indian PhD student who tricked more than 70 girls into sharing explicit images by posing online as a teenage boy, has been
articles.body: 27-year-old Bilal Kazi, an Indian PhD student who tricked more than 70 girls into sharing explicit images by posing online as a teenage boy, has been jailed for 30 years. He created a fake online profile posing as a blond-haired boy called Reece. He used to chat with young girls, as young as ten, and then convinced them to believe that they were in a relationship. Then Kazi asked for sexually explicit photos and if they refused, he used to threaten them.A court heard that one 13-year-old victim attempted suicide after Kazi circulated an explicit video of the victim that was seen by almost 100 of her friends. articles.title: Nigeria ends 21-day Ebola contact monitoring with no secondary transmission
articles.summary: None of the 62 contacts identified after the first case developed the disease, although 13 contacts reported fever.
articles.body:
Nigerian health authorities say they have completed a 21-day monitoring period for the 62 contacts of a person who contracted the Ebola virus, ⁠⁠with none of them falling ill.

Nigeria confirmed its first Ebola case in more than a decade on October 20 in a Swiss woman who had travelled to Uganda and then returned ‌‌to Nigeria.

The patient and her husband were evacuated to Switzerland where she recovered fully and has been discharged from hospital.

The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) said on Friday that none of the 62 contacts identified after the first case have developed the disease, with the ⁠⁠last contact just discharged.

Thirteen ⁠⁠contacts reported fever or other non-specific symptoms during monitoring, but all of them tested negative for the virus, the NCDC said.

⁠The agency added, however, that completing contact monitoring does not by itself mean the outbreak is over.

According to World Health Organization (WHO) protocols, ‌‌a country must complete a full 42-day countdown from the recovery or departure of the last confirmed ‌‌patient ‌‌before an official end-of-outbreak declaration can be made.

Ebola is highly contagious and spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person, including blood and vomit, or through contact with contaminated materials and surfaces, such as bedding and clothing.

This latest Ebola outbreak was first identified in Ituri in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) in May.

Since then, Ebola cases have been reported in eight provinces in the DRC, as well as in Uganda, France, Kenya and most recently, Nigeria.

The NCDC said seven ⁠⁠Ebola alerts across five Nigerian states over the past three weeks were ⁠⁠investigated, but all seven tested negative.

In DRC, the Ebola outbreak is the second-largest on record. It has infected more than 11,000 people and killed more than ‌‌5,000, according to government data.

There are no approved treatments or vaccines to combat the rare Bundibugyo strain of the virus, responsible for the ongoing outbreak.

articles.title: Microsoft says services still returning amid widespread outage
articles.summary: Governments, businesses, individuals were disrupted globally as server failures stretch into second day.
articles.body:
Microsoft has said its popular email and other services were improving but not fully restored more than 24 hours after a mass outage disrupted communications worldwide.

The outage , which began around 16:00 GMT on Thursday and affected users in 74 countries, was caused by overloaded servers that became “unexpectedly available,” the company reported. There was no indication of a cyberattack or malicious activity, the tech giant said on Friday.

“We’re seeing encouraging recovery progress, with service availability and email delivery performance improving across a growing portion of affected infrastructure,” the company said in a statement.

Microsoft reported that “email queues [are] significantly reduced and approaching normal levels”.

The outage affected Microsoft 365 services used by global businesses, institutions and individuals, including Outlook, Teams and Copilot, its artificial intelligence (AI) tool. It was one of the longest in Microsoft’s history and the second disruption to its services this year.

While Microsoft has not said how many people were affected by the outage, the company announced in January that it had more than 450 million Microsoft 365 commercial subscribers. The United States-based tech giant is valued at more than $3.8 trillion.

Microsoft reported midday GMT that email delivery and 365 services were improving across Europe, North America and the Asia Pacific but acknowledged that some services remained spotty.

As the outage stretched into its second day, users scrambled to navigate the outages, which caused logistical headaches and forced some operations to stall or grind to a halt.

The outage underscored how dependent institutions, businesses and people have become on a handful of tech companies providing services that power governments and global economies.

“What we do know so far is that this is first and foremost a communication risk,” said Walter Pasquarelli, a strategy adviser to governments on AI and affiliated researcher at the University of Cambridge. “It’s not just workers across businesses who cannot get access to it, but there’s lots of government services and lots of government infrastructure that actually relies on that.”

Foreign banks and financial institutions in Taiwan were hit especially hard, a ⁠trader told the news agency Reuters, as their data is emailed to overseas headquarters through Microsoft’s systems. Fax machines were used in Taipei while European exchange operator Euronext told companies to phone in their trades.

Norway’s parliament and several ministries lost access to email, while 80 to 90 Danish municipalities were reportedly affected. Rail operators in Germany, the United Kingdom and Canada said the outage impacted timetables and emailed tickets, and the UK’s massive National Health Service pivoted to using paper records.

In the United States, the House of Representatives and local governments were affected, Reuters reported.

The US Department of Defense, which relies heavily on Microsoft’s services, did not comment on whether it was affected. The Pentagon was slated to upgrade its Microsoft infrastructure starting in June in a $9.7bn deal that included access to Microsoft 365.

The server failures did not appear to shake Wall Street’s confidence in Microsoft, however, which said it would review the incident along with measures to prevent future disruptions. Microsoft’s stock was mostly flat in US market trading on Friday as the tech-heavy Nasdaq index fell slightly, led by the embattled AI company Nvidia .

articles.title: Pope thanks crowds on emotional return to ‘second home’ in Peru’s Chiclayo
articles.summary: The Chicago-born pope was welcomed by huge crowds in the coastal city, on the final leg of his South America tour.
articles.body:
Pope Leo has made an emotional return to his former diocese of Chiclayo in Peru, where large crowds welcomed their former bishop exactly one month after he had lung cancer surgery, and he thanked them for their support during his recovery.

“As I look at your faces, a prayer of thanksgiving to the Lord arises in my heart for the blessing you have been and continue to be in my life,” he said.

About 500,000 people gathered for Mass at Pampas de Pimentel, a desert park just outside of Peru’s fourth-largest city, according to estimates from the Vatican, while another million lined his motorcade route.

Before he was elected pope, Leo had spent about two decades working in Peru as a missionary priest and served as bishop of Chiclayo, where he is still known as “Padre Roberto” and where his image is ubiquitous, from 2015 to 2023.

In Chiclayo, a coastal city of about 620,000, Leo earned a reputation for staying close to poor communities during times of crisis, including when the region was hit with devastating floods and the COVID-19 pandemic.

Some had camped overnight to see him, while others walked in the hot sun to avoid bumper-to-bumper traffic to get to the open-air Mass.

As he rode in his popemobile, people in the crowd waved yellow and white Vatican flags and shouted, “The pope is from Chiclayo.”

“What a joy it is to return to Chiclayo,” said Leo at the start of his homily.

Originally from Chicago and formerly known as Robert Francis Prevost, Leo also holds Peruvian citizenship and declared the country his homeland on Wednesday.

Peru is the final stop of his 12-day, three-country South America tour, coming after visits to Argentina and Uruguay. Approximately 12 million people have come to see him at public events so far.

Last month, he underwent surgery for lung cancer, amid fears that the trip would have to be cancelled. But doctors have said the cancer was localised, had not spread, and would not require further treatment .

Leo will stay in the Chiclayo area until Sunday, leading eight events, including a private dinner with the priests he oversaw during his time as bishop.

Pope Leo arrives in the popemobile to celebrate Mass at the Pampas de Pimentel, during his return to the region where he served as bishop of Chiclayo from 2015 to 2023, as part of his 12-day trip to South America, in Pimentel, Peru, November 13, 2026 [Pilar Olivares/Reuters]

articles.title: US Air Force says it responded to 'suspected drones' over RAF Lakenheath
articles.summary: The American military says there were no injuries or damage after "suspected unauthorised drone activity" this evening.
articles.body:
The US Air Force said it responded to "suspected unauthorised drone activity" over RAF Lakenheath in Suffolk on Friday evening.

No personnel, aircraft or infrastructure were affected, a spokesperson for the US Air Force said.

It comes after unconfirmed reports that sirens were sounded at the base, which residents reported hearing from a nearby village.

A Ministry of Defence spokesperson told the BBC it was "coordinating with all relevant parties", adding that US Air Force security personnel responded to the reports and the situation was resolved.

"We are working closely with them to establish the facts," they added.

West Suffolk MP Nick Timothy said he had been in touch with authorities at the base, and was told "there is no threat to the public, and the incident is now resolved".

"Given the raised threat level, I continue to encourage everyone to report anything suspicious or out of the ordinary to the authorities," he added in a social media post.

Earlier this week, at least 12 US Air Force aircraft departed the nearby RAF Mildenhall base.

They included two Boeing Stratotanker KC-135 refuelling aircraft, with one apparently headed towards Germany and another seen landing at Prestwick Airport near Glasgow.

There has been heightened security activity at US bases in the UK following an incident at RAF Fairford in September that Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Iran played a part in.

Police said petrol but no explosives were found during searches of vans near the base.

Two men have been charged by the Crown Prosecution Service over their alleged involvement in the incident.

While Iran denied any responsibility, the US removed all of its bombers from the base in October.

The Wall Street Journal reported the departure of the US aircraft from RAF Mildenhall this week was in response to a further threat from Iran but the BBC has not independently verified the claim.

Earlier this week, Downing Street insisted British airbases were safe and that their security is a "top priority".

RAF Lakenheath hosts the US Air Force's 48th Fighter Wing, or the Liberty Wing as it is also known, which has nearly 7,000 active-duty personnel, some of whom are stationed at the base.

The Liberty Wing is the largest US fighter operation in Europe, its website says, employing four combat ready fighter squadrons.

articles.title: New Orleans boat crash called ‘miracle on the Mississippi’ as everyone is accounted for, officials say
articles.summary: Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry called it "a literal miracle on the Mississippi" after a tanker capsized the American Heritage cruiser in New Orleans.
articles.body: Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry called it "a literal miracle on the Mississippi" Friday after officials said everyone was accounted for following a tanker collision that capsized a docked New Orleans river cruiser and sent 32 passengers to hospitals. "This is a miracle," Landry said at a news conference. "The Mississippi River is not some quiet pond, right? I mean, there were challenges out there." Mayor Helena Moreno said none of the hospitalized passengers had critical injuries. Two Harbor Police officers were also hospitalized and were in good condition, officials said. CRUISE PASSENGER HAILED AS HERO AFTER JUMPING INTO WATER TO SAVE 84-YEAR-OLD MAN "We have zero people unaccounted for, which is a miracle," Moreno said, crediting local, state and federal responders who jumped into the water to help. Coast Guard Capt. Melanie Burnham confirmed the search-and-rescue operation had ended. TEEN BOATER FOUND CLINGING TO CAPSIZED VESSEL AFTER 3 GO MISSING; 2 BODIES RECOVERED "We got everybody," Landry added. Officials said the tanker lost control before striking the American Heritage. Passengers were evacuating when the cruiser began taking on water and capsized, leaving some people in the river and others on a portion of the vessel still above water. MOM LOSES GRIP ON DAUGHTER AS PASSENGER FERRY CAPSIZES WITH 20 PEOPLE STILL MISSING Harbor Police responded first, firefighters lowered ladders over the dock and nearby vessels helped pull people from the water. New Orleans Police Superintendent Anne Kirkpatrick said a police drone already airborne for an unrelated theft call was redirected to the scene within moments. Landry said the incident remains under active investigation. Burnham said investigators were examining an apparent loss of steering, but the exact cause was not yet known. The National Transportation Safety Board said on X that it was launching a Go Team to investigate the collision, with investigators expected to arrive Saturday morning. Board Member John DeLeeuw will serve as the spokesperson on scene, and details of media briefings will be announced once confirmed, the agency said. 11-NIGHT CARIBBEAN CRUISE ABRUPTLY CANCELED AFTER COAST GUARD DETAINS SHIP The Atlantic Asphalt tanker struck American Cruise Lines’ American Heritage around 12:30 p.m. on the Mississippi River, the Port of New Orleans said in a statement shared with Fox News. Port officials initially reported about 129 passengers, in addition to crew members, aboard. Moreno later estimated roughly 180 to 190 people were on the ship. University Medical Center New Orleans and other LCMC Health hospitals had earlier received an estimated two dozen patients following the incident, LCMC Health said in a statement. Medical teams were evaluating patients and providing care while coordinating with emergency responders. Moreno subsequently announced the updated total of 32 hospitalized passengers. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the Coast Guard was supporting state and local responders near mile marker 96 on the Mississippi River. "We are throwing every asset we have to help rescue missing passengers," Mullin wrote on X, adding that DHS was coordinating closely with Louisiana officials. "Our prayers are with all those impacted by this terrible tragedy." TWO DEAD, INCLUDING INFANT, AFTER BOAT CAPSIZES IN NEW YORK HARBOR; 12 RESCUED American Cruise Lines confirmed that guests and crew were evacuated and said it was coordinating closely with the U.S. Coast Guard and local authorities. "Guests and crew were evacuated, and we are deeply concerned for everyone involved," the company said in a statement. "We will share more information as it becomes available." The United Cajun Navy said on X that it was on standby at the port. The New Orleans Fire Department and NOLA Ready said in an earlier Facebook update that multiple people had been rescued and search-and-rescue operations were ongoing at the time of the post. Acadian Ambulance said in an earlier update on X that it had transported eight patients and had 15 units and two sprint trucks on scene to assist New Orleans EMS and other first responders. The ambulance service said it was prepared to send additional units if needed. Port NOLA Harbor Police, the New Orleans Fire Department, the New Orleans Police Department, the U.S. Coast Guard and emergency medical personnel were on scene conducting rescue and response operations. AT LEAST 40 RESCUED, 2 DEAD AS BOAT CAPSIZES AFTER MACHETE FIGHT NEAR PUERTO RICO Passengers were brought inside the Port of New Orleans Administration Building for triage and assistance, officials said. Moreno said crews conducted roll calls and checked hospital lists to account for everyone. Officials were arranging hotel rooms, transportation, replacement prescriptions and ways for passengers to contact relatives after losing phones, identification and other belongings. The Red Cross and medical partners were helping, Moreno said. She said no children were aboard and no injuries were reported on the tanker. The American Heritage had docked about two hours before the collision to begin letting passengers off. According to the news release, skies were clear with no precipitation around the time of the collision, with temperatures in the upper 60s and north winds of 8 to 12 mph, gusting to 15 to 17 mph. The release listed the current water temperature at around 66 degrees. At the news conference, Landry said Moreno called him in Baton Rouge to request resources. He contacted Mullin before President Donald Trump called to offer whatever assistance Louisiana needed. Landry said the state would continue helping until passengers were able to return home. Rep. Troy Carter, D-La., said he was closely monitoring the response. "I am devastated to hear about the ships crashing near the Port of New Orleans," Carter wrote on X. "I am monitoring the situation closely and praying for the swift rescue of survivors and for all emergency crews responding to the situation." Rep. Julia Letlow, R-La., also offered prayers for passengers and first responders. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Praying for a successful rescue mission by the dedicated first responders on the scene near the Port of New Orleans, and for the health and safety of all passengers affected," Letlow wrote on X. NOLA Ready, the city’s emergency preparedness agency, urged people to avoid the area and allow responders to work.

articles.title: Father of 20-year-old co-pilot Nathalia Filgueiras killed in Florida Learjet crash calls her a ‘hero’; says listening to final radio transmissions was ‘extremely painful’; ‘I need some answers to find peace’
articles.summary: The father of 20-year-old co-pilot Nathalia Filgueiras, who was among nine people killed when a Learjet crashed onto a Florida highway earlier this month,
articles.body: The father of 20-year-old co-pilot Nathalia Filgueiras, who was among nine people killed when a Learjet crashed onto a Florida highway earlier this month, has described his daughter as a hero and said he is desperately waiting for answers about what led to the tragedy. Allan Filgueiras, an experienced pilot himself, said listening to his daughter's final radio communications with air traffic control has been extremely painful, but has also given him an insight into her courage during the aircraft's final moments.In an interview with ABC News' Rhiannon Ally that aired on Thursday's edition of ‘Good Morning America’, Allan said he had listened to the recordings made as the Learjet encountered difficult weather conditions during its flight from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas on November 1.According to the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB), the aircraft's two-person crew reported icing on the plane and moderate turbulence before the jet began a rapid descent from 35,000 feet and issued a Mayday call to air traffic control.Father recalls daughter's final moments in the cockpitNathalia was serving as the co-pilot and was responsible for communicating with air traffic control as the aircraft encountered increasingly difficult conditions. Pilot Jeff Gregory, 55, was also in the cockpit when the crew reported problems, requested a better route and eventually began an emergency descent.The aircraft subsequently crashed near West Palm Beach, killing both pilots and all seven passengers.Recalling the experience of listening to the final transmissions, Allan said it was difficult to hear what his daughter had gone through.“It felt like she was alone, trying to recover an aircraft that ... was un-recoverable,” he said.Despite the heartbreak, he said he could hear his daughter's courage in the recordings and believes she did everything she could during the emergency.NTSB investigates possible damage to Learjet's tail sectionThe NTSB is investigating the circumstances surrounding the crash. At a news conference last week, investigators revealed that the aircraft's left elevator, a control surface located on the tail, had been recovered in three pieces. Some of the fragments were found nearly four miles from the crash site.An NTSB official said investigators have not yet determined whether the loss of the left elevator contributed to the crash or whether the extreme forces experienced by the aircraft as it descended caused the component to break apart.The jet was a 22-year-old twin-engine Learjet 60. Investigators are examining the available evidence to establish what happened during the aircraft's final flight.‘I need some answers to try to find peace,’ says grieving fatherAllan has defended his daughter's abilities as a pilot, describing her as exceptionally talented and qualified to be part of the flight crew. He said her young age should not take away from her professional capabilities.“There is no age to exercise a gift, and she did,” he said. “She was gifted.”The grieving father is now working with a legal team as he seeks further information about the aircraft and the circumstances surrounding the accident. His attorneys, Andrew Yaffa and Stuart Grossman, have said they want to examine the plane and review its maintenance records.For now, Allan said he is waiting for the NTSB's findings and wants investigators to establish what led the crew to fly through the difficult weather conditions.“I want to hear what the NTSB has to say,” he said.Father questions why the aircraft did not avoid the stormAsked what he hoped to learn from the investigation, Allan acknowledged that no explanation could bring his daughter back. However, he said understanding why the aircraft followed the route it did was important to finding some measure of peace.“Why did they go where they went?” he asked.He questioned why the crew did not take an alternative route to avoid the weather, pointing out that pilots have several resources available to them when navigating difficult flying conditions.“Flying a jet, you have so many resources. You had 20 minutes, you had 30 minutes, and you go around the weather,” he said.Allan also stressed that his daughter was a responsible pilot and not someone who would take unnecessary risks.“And she was so responsible. She was not a cowboy-style pilot. ... So why they didn't go around? What made them go through the routes that they went? I have a lot of questions,” he said.Nine people died in the Florida Learjet crashThe November 1 crash claimed the lives of both pilots and seven passengers. The passengers were identified as Anita Maria Cetina, Charmi Fehr, Rachael Reed, Adam Robinson, his wife Helen Sharp and their two young children, Emma and Charlie.The NTSB investigation remains ongoing. Allan said he is waiting for investigators to establish what caused the aircraft to descend rapidly and crash, hoping the findings will provide answers about the final moments of his daughter's life.You use AI every day. articles.title: Connecticut teacher escorted out of school over classroom crucifix heads to federal appeals court
articles.summary: Marisol Arroyo-Castro says she was escorted out of her Connecticut public school after refusing to remove a crucifix she displayed for a decade, while her school district says the story is more complicated.
articles.body: A veteran Connecticut public school teacher who says she was escorted out of her school with a crucifix in a box after refusing to remove the religious symbol from her classroom is taking her First Amendment fight to a federal appeals court, with oral arguments scheduled for Dec. 7. Marisol Arroyo-Castro, who has taught for more than 30 years, told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview that she was stunned when a school administrator informed her that displaying the crucifix was illegal and warned that refusing to remove it would amount to insubordination. "I said, 'I can't,'" Arroyo-Castro said, remembering the moment she was told she could return to her classroom only if she left the crucifix behind. CHRISTIAN TEACHER WAS 'QUITE SHOCKED' AFTER GETTING FIRED FOR TELLING STUDENT SHE'S PRO-LIFE The confrontation sparked a legal battle over religious expression in public schools, with Arroyo-Castro's attorneys arguing that her personal display was protected by the First Amendment and the school district maintaining a position that prevailed in federal district court. The dispute began in December 2024, after administrators at DiLoreto Elementary & Middle School in New Britain, Connecticut, ordered Arroyo-Castro to remove a crucifix she had displayed near her desk for roughly a decade. Arroyo-Castro, who was teaching middle-school social studies, said the crucifix had been a quiet source of comfort throughout her career, something she would look at while grading papers or completing reports. "I pretty much kept it to myself," she said. "It keeps me calm and [it's] just part of me." But when administrators pressed her to move it, she said she broke down in tears. "I just started to cry and cry and cry," she recalled. "They just backed away little by little until they left the room, and they left me there crying." NASHVILLE SCHOOL PULLS LGBT BOOKS AFTER CHRISTIAN TEACHER WAS DISCIPLINED FOR REFUSING TO READ ONE On Dec. 11, 2024, she received a formal reprimand for insubordination, and the following day, school officials removed the crucifix and suspended her for two days without pay. She was placed on paid administrative leave on Dec. 16, 2024, and reassigned to a non-teaching role in March 2025. Arroyo-Castro filed a federal lawsuit in January 2025, alleging violations of her First Amendment rights. A federal judge denied her request for a preliminary injunction in November 2025, finding she was unlikely to prevail because the classroom display constituted government speech. Her attorneys appealed to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit, where the dispute over her request for preliminary relief remains the subject of the appeal described in their March 2026 brief. "They suspended me," Arroyo-Castro told Fox News Digital. "Then they told me that they were going to pay me after that, but that I couldn't go back into the school near the children, that they didn't want me around the students, that I'm not supposed to talk to the students or interact with them or any of the staff in the school. Things like that, like I was a pariah or something." JUDGE ORDERS WASHINGTON SCHOOL DISTRICT TO LOOSEN LIMITS ON OFF-CAMPUS BIBLE CLUB FOR PUBLIC SCHOOL STUDENTS Becky Rees Dummermuth, senior counsel at First Liberty Institute, told Fox News Digital in an interview that the case is ongoing. "So we've appealed to the Second Circuit Court of Appeals, and in the next couple of weeks, on Dec. 7, we'll have an oral argument there in the Second Circuit Court of Appeals in New York City, and we'll argue before the court that Marisol's speech was private speech. And the Supreme Court said in its Kennedy decision a few years ago, made really clear that a teacher's private religious expression is allowable even if students are able to see it." The Kennedy decision refers to football coach Joe Kennedy having his right upheld by the Supreme Court to pray publicly without fear of retribution. Dummermuth said that Arroyo-Castro's attorneys will argue her display of the crucifix was protected under the First Amendment's Free Exercise and Free Speech Clauses, adding that public schools must treat teachers equally, arguing that if other educators are permitted to display personal items near their desks, religious expression should not be singled out for exclusion. VIRGINIA STATE UNIVERSITY ACCUSED OF SUPPRESSING CHRISTIAN STUDENT MINISTRIES WHILE MUSLIM GROUPS ARE EXEMPT In a statement to Fox News Digital, a spokesperson for the Consolidated School District of New Britain said, "The Consolidated School District of New Britain has consistently maintained that this matter extends beyond the presence of a religious symbol in a classroom. As outlined in the attached independent, third-party investigative report, the district's concerns involved a broader pattern of statements and actions that raised serious concerns about the treatment of students of differing religious backgrounds." The spokesperson continued, "The district respects the religious beliefs and individual rights of all students and staff. However, we also have a legal and ethical responsibility to ensure that every classroom remains an inclusive and welcoming environment where students of all faiths and backgrounds feel respected and valued." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The spokesperson added, "Throughout this process, we have operated in good faith and provided multiple options to Ms. Castro, which she and her attorneys have declined. Ms. Castro was offered a variety of ways in which she could practice her faith while not encroaching on the religious freedoms of her students. "She declined all of the options that were provided to her. We will continue to follow legal guidance as we move forward, and we remain steadfast in our duty to uphold both the law and the values of inclusion, neutrality, and respect for all of our students and families." The district's referenced third-party report obtained by Fox News Digital included interviews with four teachers and the school's principal and assistant principal, as well as Castro herself. It also reiterated several students' claims that she referenced God, Jesus and religion in a matter the investigator concluded was inappropriate. It included Castro's denial that she made such references "during a class." The teachers interviewed in the report also criticized Castro's classroom management and treatment of students. First Liberty responded, "The school district repeatedly told Ms. Castro that she could return to the classroom if she simply took down the crucifix. When they removed her from the classroom, the only concern they mentioned was preventing an alleged Establishment Clause violation, a baseless concern that cannot survive the Supreme Court’s Kennedy decision."

articles.title: Three demolition workers found a hidden pot of gold coins worth €240,000 beneath a Belgian house; they divided and sold the treasure, but a court later found all three guilty of theft
articles.summary: Three demolition workers in Belgium discovered a hidden pot of gold coins while dismantling an old house in 2019.
articles.body: Three demolition workers in Belgium discovered a hidden pot of gold coins while dismantling an old house in 2019. But what appeared to be a stroke of luck eventually brought them before a criminal court. The coins were estimated to be worth €240,000. Instead of reporting the discovery, the workers divided the treasure among themselves and sold part of it. Their actions came to light after rumours spread about the find, prompting the former homeowner's family to report the matter to authorities and triggering a lengthy legal investigation.Belgian demolition workers found €240,000 worth of gold during demolitionThe discovery took place in October 2019 in Assebroek, a suburb of Bruges, when three construction workers were carrying out demolition work on an old property. According to The Brussels Times report of June 2025, the workers uncovered a pot of gold coins in a concealed space beneath the cellar while accessing the area with a crane.The workers were identified as F.M., 46, from Zedelgem, T.D., 46, from Ypres, and P.K., 50, from Oostkamp. The hidden compartment was not part of the demolition plans, making the discovery unexpected.The coins included South African Krugerrands and Belgian ECU pieces. The ECU was a European currency unit used before the introduction of the euro. The value of the collection was estimated at €240,000, although the amount eventually realised by the workers through sales was considerably lower.How the former homeowner's family found about the missing treasureThe house had previously belonged to an elderly woman who sold the property in 2018 before moving into a care home. She was reportedly 93 years old when the discovery became the subject of the legal proceedings.The Brussels Times reported that the former owners had not known the coins were still hidden inside the house when they sold it. The treasure was concealed behind a safe, and the woman had apparently forgotten about it.The discovery became public after one of the workers shared information about it, with a witness eventually telling neighbours about a bag of jewellery. The family subsequently filed a complaint in 2020, seeking to recover the value of the gold.The gold coins were divided and sold among the workersInvestigators later established that the workers had divided the coins rather than informing the former homeowner or the authorities about their discovery.The Brussels Times reported that F.M. sold 12 South African Krugerrands and 55 Belgian ECU coins in Antwerp for €52,000. The sale involved 67 coins in total, providing investigators with a clear trail linking the discovery to the money received.T.D. also sold his share of the coins for €30,000. That money was reportedly spent on cars and gambling. P.K. received a considerably smaller share, consisting of one gold coin and €2,000.Why the discovery became a criminal caseThe legal dispute centred on whether the coins belonged to the former homeowner or should be treated as a hidden treasure discovered during construction work.When the three workers appeared before the Bruges Correctional Court in June 2025, their lawyers argued that the discovery did not amount to theft. They maintained that the men had not intended to steal anything and that the coins should instead be treated as a treasure found accidentally.The defence also argued that the former homeowner no longer owned the property when the coins were discovered. According to The Brussels Times, lawyer Bart Bleyaert maintained that the treasure should be divided between its discoverers and the new property owner under the rules governing hidden valuables.The former owner's representatives rejected that interpretation and demanded €240,000 in compensation. They argued that the woman was entitled to the coins and had lost their full value because the workers sold them.Bruges court found all three demolition workers guiltyThe case eventually reached its end on 16 September 2025, when the Bruges Criminal Court found all three workers guilty of stealing and selling the gold coins.The Brussels Times reported that the verdict followed a lengthy investigation that had delayed the proceedings. Although the men had admitted discovering the coins, the central question was whether their subsequent actions amounted to criminal theft. The court's decision established that the discovery could not simply be treated as an opportunity for the workers to divide and sell the valuables themselves.You use AI every day.
