articles.title: A 13-inch sculpture model that Barbara Hepworth gave her doctor has resurfaced for auction in Cornwall, where the aluminium-and-string study for her famous Winged Figure could fetch as much as £80,000
articles.summary: Explore the fascinating story behind a miniature 13-inch sculpture model by Barbara Hepworth, gifted to her doctor, which is set to auction for up to £80,000 in Cornwall.
articles.body: Few people consider doctors to be an imitation of God. Not sure about God, but doctors certainly hold a special place of trust and respect in people's hearts. And sometimes, the relationship between a doctor and a patient extends far beyond the consulting room. Something similar happened between British sculptor Barbara Hepworth and her doctor, Roger Slack. Their friendship eventually became so meaningful that Hepworth gifted him a miniature sculpture of one of her most celebrated works. Nearly six decades later, that very sculpture has resurfaced and could fetch as much as £80,000 at an auction in Cornwall.The 13-inch (33 cm) aluminium-and-string sculpture is a miniature version of Hepworth's famous Winged Figure, which stands on the exterior of the John Lewis department store on Oxford Street, London. The artwork, signed and dated 1967 and numbered 5/9, was gifted to Dr Slack as a personal token of appreciation. According to the original auction listing published by Lay's Auctioneers, the sculpture will be offered as part of its Cornish Art sale on November 26 and 27, 2026.A friendship that went beyond the doctor's clinicWhen Roger Slack arrived in St Ives in 1947 as a general practitioner, he soon found himself treating some of Britain's most celebrated artists, including Barbara Hepworth, Peter Lanyon, Patrick Heron and Terry Frost. But his relationship with them was not limited to medical appointments. Irish painter Tony O'Malley, for instance, reportedly had his life saved several times by Slack, and the two eventually became close friends.Slack was equally fascinated by the artistic life of the town. In the 1950s, he began photographing St Ives and recording the memories of elderly residents who had known painter Alfred Wallis, a self-taught artist. Hepworth took a particular interest in his work and encouraged him to write a book about Wallis. She also shared some of her marble with Slack, who had an interest in sculpture himself.Over the years, the friendship between the Slacks and Hepworth grew beyond the doctor-patient relationship. As a gesture of their friendship and mutual appreciation, Hepworth gifted Roger the miniature Winged Figure, making it a personal reminder of the bond they had developed over years of shared interests and affection.The art behind the famous Winged FigureTo understand why this small sculpture is attracting such attention, it helps to look at the artwork that inspired it.In 1961, Hepworth received a commission from the John Lewis Partnership to create a sculpture for its flagship department store on Oxford Street. She was selected for the project over six other sculptors. Her final design was an enlargement of an earlier work from 1957, also titled Winged Figure.The monumental sculpture was completed in 1963 and stands nearly six metres tall on the exterior of the department store. Made from aluminium with metal rods, its form consists of two sweeping, wing-like structures connected by slender lines. The openings and curves create an interesting play of light and shadow, making the sculpture appear different as the light changes throughout the day.Hepworth wanted the work to communicate a feeling of freedom and movement. In 1963, she explained that she wanted to evoke the universal dream of moving through air and water without the resistance of human legs. The sculpture was her attempt to translate that sensation into a physical form. The work has since become a familiar landmark on Oxford Street. It was also granted Grade II listed status in 2016, recognising its architectural and historic significance.Why is a 13-inch sculpture worth £80,000?The price is not simply about its size or the materials used to make it. Several factors contribute to its estimated value as well. First, it is the work of Barbara Hepworth, one of Britain's most influential modern sculptors, whose works are held in major museums and collections around the world. Her sculptures are particularly recognised for exploring the relationship between form, space, light and natural surroundings.Secondly, the miniature has a direct connection to Winged Figure, one of her most recognisable public commissions. It offers collectors an opportunity to own a smaller version of an artistic idea that became a major London landmark.Its rarity also matters. The sculpture belongs to an edition of just nine, making it a relatively uncommon work. More importantly, its provenance, or documented ownership history, adds another layer of significance. This particular sculpture was gifted by Hepworth herself to Dr Slack, making its connection to the artist personal as well as artistic.The accompanying history of the gift makes the artwork especially interesting to collectors. It connects Hepworth's artistic career with the community of St Ives, where she spent much of her life and developed friendships with fellow artists and local residents. As it returns to the auction market, the miniature Winged Figure brings together two stories: the artistic vision behind one of Britain's best-known modern sculptures and the personal friendship that led its creator to give a piece of that work away.You use AI every day. articles.title: Probation officers to take industrial action over pay and early release scheme
articles.summary: It comes as prisons prepare to free more inmates early in the coming months.
articles.body:
Probation officers have voted to reject a 5% pay rise and take industrial action, citing growing pressure created by the government's prisoner early release scheme.

Members of Napo, the probation service union, voted to refuse overtime from 23 November - and could take strike action should the union "deem that option to be necessary".

Its general secretary Ian Lawrence said the service was "already in crisis" before the early release scheme came into force, which relies on probation staff monitoring freed prisoners in the community.

A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said the government had put forward a "strong offer" and was recruiting an extra "1,300 officers to significantly cut workloads".

They added that the government has "robust contingency plans in place" to ensure offenders "are still subject to the same rigorous supervision" in the event of industrial action.

Probation service unions have warned that officers have too many cases and the rate at which staff are leaving the profession has increased.

The service has come under renewed pressure in recent months as a result of the early release scheme, the union said, which the government introduced as prisons were dangerously close to capacity.

Seven-hundred eligible offenders originally sentenced to up to 19 months were released on 1 October, with another two groups of 650 prisoners released on 13 October and 10 November.

Another nine groups are expected to leave prison in the next seven months, with inmates who received longer sentences included in the later cohorts.

Some 250 prisoners serving more than 12 years are expected to be released on 9 June.

Napo's leader said staff had tried "desperately" to implement early release schemes introduced by the Labour government and previous Conservative government, but had been asked to do so with "inadequate staff and a lack of resources".

The government has said electronic tags and probation intervention will help to manage prisoners freed early.

The Probation Service uses electronic monitoring to track curfews and conditions of a court or prison order, with most of those eligible for early release now requiring tagging.

But a September report by His Majesty's Inspectorate of Probation (HMIP) found that almost half of electronic tags used to track offenders' movements were not fitted on time .

articles.title: Celebrity and humanitarian advocates of persecuted Nigerian Christians hope for continued attention to crisis
articles.summary: Advocates for persecuted Christians in Nigeria are concerned over lack of headlines and a potential change in support from DC after the midterms.
articles.body: While humanitarian groups and celebrities have condemned attacks on Nigerian Christians, reports of renewed violence in the country's Middle Belt and concerns about the political fallout from the U.S. midterm elections have raised concerns about the future of religious-freedom efforts. Advocates question whether the violence will subside and hope for more attention to the crisis. "Things have gotten worse," Stephen Osemwegie, president and founder of Save Nigeria Group USA, a nonprofit focused on the welfare of Nigerians in America and around the world, told Fox News Digital. "So as far as the scale, yes, people are still getting killed, but it's not making the news because the U.S. is a bit distracted." He said millions of people remain displaced, churches continue to be vandalized and destroyed, and parishioners are being killed while the war in Iran and the recent midterm elections have dominated U.S. headlines. BISHOP ROBERT BARRON: THE WAR ON CHRISTIANS IS REAL AND THE WORLD CAN NO LONGER STAY SILENT While religious and communal strife has existed for decades, the violent conflict involving Islamist insurgencies began around 2009. Since then, the United Nations and Armed Conflict & Location Data Project (ACLED), which monitors conflict and protest, reports that violence across Nigeria has claimed upwards of 53,000+ lives across communities. Advocacy and human rights groups like Intersociety and Open Doors report that over 50,000 to 62,000 Christians have been killed since 2009. Beyond humanitarian organizations, Christian leaders and church groups, celebrities such as rapper Nicki Minaj and actress Patricia Heaton have repeatedly addressed the crisis publicly. In October, during an X Takeover event at Tesla's Giga Texas facility, Minaj spoke about her personal connection to Nigeria and urged fellow celebrities, influencers and Christians to raise awareness of the crisis. In November 2025, she joined U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz at an event titled "Combatting Religious Violence and the Killing of Christians in Nigeria," where she delivered remarks and thanked President Donald Trump for his efforts prioritizing the issue, combatting extremism and trying to put a stop to violence to those who want to exercise their natural right to freedom of religion or belief. "I stand here as a proud New Yorker with a deep sense of gratitude that we live in a country where we can freely and safely worship God regardless of one's creed, background or politics. No group should ever be persecuted for practicing their religion…," Minaj said. "In Nigeria, Christians are being targeted, driven from their homes and killed. Churches have been burned, families have been torn apart, and entire communities live in fear constantly simply because of how they pray." NIGERIAN PASTOR HIGHLIGHTED BY TRUMP SAYS HE’S NEXT AFTER MILITIA KILLS HIS RELATIVES Likewise, Heaton has shared social media posts and news commentary about reported massacres, beheadings and mass burials. She has also criticized what she sees as insufficient media coverage and international attention. In May, she wrote "Pray for our brothers and sisters" while re-posting a video by Jeremy Wayne Tate noting that more than 70% of all Christians killed for their faith last year were Nigerian. US, NIGERIA STRIKE ISIS FIGHTERS AGAIN FROM THE AIR AFTER KILLING SENIOR LEADER Fox News Digital reached out to both Minaj and Heaton for additional comment. Violence stemming from clashes and attacks by radical Islamist groups, including Boko Haram and Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP), as well as Fulani ethnic militias, has intensified since the 2010s. Attacks have increasingly extended into Nigeria's Middle Belt, targeting farming and Christian communities, while the crisis exists within a broader national conflict that has affected communities across religious lines, including Muslims and others. Organizations such as Open Doors International that monitor the crisis report that thousands of Christians have been displaced and forced into camps within the country. Meanwhile, Sahara Reporters cited an October report by Aid to the Church in Need that said more than 3.5 million people had been displaced in Nigeria. articles.title: A UK woman died of breast cancer at 46, leaving her £500,000 estate to her teenage daughter; her boyfriend later claimed a secret Cyprus marriage and produced a will that the High Court found to be forged
articles.summary: A family inheritance dispute in the UK has ended with a High Court ruling against a man who claimed he had secretly married his dying partner in Cyprus
articles.body: A family inheritance dispute in the UK has ended with a High Court ruling against a man who claimed he had secretly married his dying partner in Cyprus and was entitled to her fortune of more than £500,000, as reported by The Independent. Cengiz Arif produced a marriage certificate and a later will that supposedly left him the entire estate of Kassy Sinar, who died of breast cancer aged 46. However, her family challenged both documents, prompting an investigation into their authenticity. The judge ultimately found that the marriage certificate and the 2023 will were forged, upholding Sinar's earlier will that secured the inheritance for her teenage daughter.Mother's death leaves £500,000 estate for teenage daughter amid family disputeKassy Sinar, who ran a cleaning business, died in October 2023 after being diagnosed with breast cancer. She was 46. Her daughter, Jocey, was 14 when she lost her mother. Sinar had made arrangements for her daughter's future in a will drawn up in 2022, leaving her estate in a trust for Jocey's benefit.Sinar owned a home in Kimberley Gardens, Finsbury Park, London, where she had settled after moving from Manchester. She also had a property on Thurston Street in Burnley, reportedly worth around £58,000. The estate was believed to be worth more than £500,000, though its exact value was not established during the legal proceedings.Her relationship with Jocey's father, Cengiz Arif, had not always been straightforward. They were together for several years but separated at different points between 2011 and 2018 before getting back together. Evidence heard in court included accounts of Sinar telling people close to her that she had rejected a marriage proposal from Arif. Some friends also described their relationship as toxic and abusive, alleging that she had faced physical and emotional mistreatment.They later reconciled, but the relationship between Arif and Sinar's relatives became a source of dispute following her death. What followed was a legal disagreement over her estate and the arrangements she had made for her daughter.Boyfriend claims they had married in Cyprus years earlierFollowing Sinar's death, Arif said that he had actually been her husband for years. He produced a marriage certificate claiming that the couple had married in Cyprus on September 19, 2006. According to his account, the ceremony had taken place without her close relatives or friends being informed.The claim raised questions within Sinar's family, particularly because nobody in her immediate circle appeared to have known about the alleged wedding. Her brother, Ernest Sinar, began investigating the document and contacted Turkish authorities to establish whether the marriage had been registered as claimed.Questions were also raised about the marriage certificate Arif had produced. Authorities reportedly confirmed that no marriage had been registered on the date mentioned in the document. The registrar named on the certificate was not working at the time either. The information shared with the family further suggested that the marriage had no legal standing.The tensions had affected the family long before the inheritance case reached its conclusion. Sinar's relatives were banned by Arif from attending her funeral in London, so they organised a separate memorial service. In the months that followed, her brother Ernest and his wife Michelle took Jocey into their care and became her legal guardians.Man challenges daughter's inheritance with a second will dated May 2023The inheritance dispute took a different turn when Arif brought forward another document. Dated May 10, 2023, the will was presented as Sinar's final wishes. It differed sharply from the 2022 version, which had placed her estate in a trust for Jocey. Under the newer document, Arif stood to receive the entire estate instead.This included Sinar's two properties and the income they generated. Arif had also started collecting rent from the Finsbury Park house. More than £35,000 in rental payments was reportedly held in a bank account under his control. He disputed the earlier will, too. His argument centred on changes Sinar had made to the document after it was first prepared and signed. He questioned whether those amendments affected its validity.Sinar's brother Ernest challenged Arif's claims. He maintained that his sister had wanted Jocey to benefit from her estate and questioned the circumstances in which the later will had supposedly been drawn up.The family disagreement eventually reached court. At the heart of the case was a question that would determine who inherited Sinar's estate: which of the two wills, if either, reflected her actual wishes?Handwriting evidence raises questions about the 2023 willChief Master Karen Shuman had to examine both wills and the circumstances in which they were drawn up. Arif did not appear at the hearing to defend his position. The court ultimately accepted the 2022 will. According to Rothley Law, Sinar had appointed four executors in her 2022 will, including Ernest and Arif. In early October 2023, she amended the will to remove Arif as an executor.There were also questions over the signature on the later document. A handwriting expert who examined it identified features suggesting an attempt had been made to copy Sinar's handwriting. The judge weighed this against Arif's explanation of how May 2023 would have come about.In her ruling, Chief Master Shuman found that the May 2023 will was forged. The marriage certificate Arif had produced was also found to be false. That meant his claim to have been Sinar's husband was rejected, along with his attempt to inherit under the disputed document.Judge removes boyfriend from control of the estateThe ruling restored the arrangements made under Sinar's 2022 will, leaving her estate in trust for Jocey. Arif was removed from his positions as executor and trustee, ending his authority over the assets. The judge was also concerned about the money already collected from the London property's rental income and the possibility that estate assets could be moved or spent. She issued an injunction preventing Arif from dealing with or disposing of the properties and funds.His bank was ordered to disclose information about the rental payments to Ernest's legal representatives. The restrictions were intended to protect the estate while its financial position was established. Chief Master Shuman expressed concern about the use of what she found to be forged documents in support of Arif's inheritance claim, as well as his failure to comply with court orders. She considered restrictions on his access to the estate necessary to prevent further difficulties in recovering its assets.£206,000 legal costs ordered against ArifThe court proceedings also resulted in a substantial financial order against Arif. He was directed to pay the legal costs incurred by Ernest in bringing the challenge, which were estimated at approximately £206,000. An immediate payment of £120,000 was ordered towards those costs, with the remaining amount forming part of the wider costs order.Following the judgment, Verity Hudson of Rothley Law, the firm representing Ernest, described the proceedings as a complex and emotionally difficult matter. She said the legal team had worked closely with the family since 2023 and welcomed the outcome.Disclaimer: This article is based on publicly available reports and statements from the sources cited.
